summary: This document specifies the Host Access Protocol, designed as the network-access protocol for the Wideband Packet Satellite Network and intended to evolve toward other networks such as SATNET. The RFC itself calls HAP an experimental protocol that would be revised.

plainLanguage.summary: HAP defines how a computer sends data and control messages to the satellite network switch connected to it. The switch then carries data to other hosts, using either ordinary messages or prearranged streams.

subtitle: A host-to-network protocol for sending messages through packet-switched satellite systems.

tldr.problem: A computer connected to a packet satellite network needs a defined way to exchange data and control messages with its local satellite switch.
tldr.mechanism: HAP defines 16-bit-word datagrams, reserved-bandwidth streams, group delivery, setup exchanges, and optional acceptance or refusal feedback on the host-to-SIMP link.
tldr.outcome: The RFC describes HAP as experimental and subject to revision. Unit metadata lists RFC 907 as an Internet Standard updated by RFC 1221.

sections.title: The Host and Its Satellite Network Link
sections.content:
The Host Access Protocol (HAP) governs communication between a host computer and its local Satellite Interface Message Processor (SIMP). The SIMP connects that host to a packet-switched satellite network and routes messages to destination hosts.

HAP defines data and control message formats and explains when each message is sent. It assumes a lower-level link protocol can provide reliable exchange when the host-to-SIMP link needs it.
sections.plainLanguage: HAP is the set of rules a host and its local satellite switch use to exchange messages. Another link protocol can handle reliable delivery between those two devices.

sections.title: Datagrams, Streams and Groups
sections.content:
HAP carries two kinds of host-to-host data. A datagram is an independent message; a stream uses a channel allocation arranged before data flows. The RFC gives a nominal delay of about 0.6 seconds for a datagram crossing two satellite hops and about 0.3 seconds for a stream crossing one hop.

Streams suit volatile traffic such as speech or applications that need guaranteed channel bandwidth. Their message size and timing must fit the allocation. Hosts also have permanent 16-bit logical addresses and can send to a group address for delivery to group members.

HAP does not guarantee error-free, ordered delivery. The host can choose a reliability level and whether to discard data when the network detects errors.
sections.plainLanguage: A datagram is a single message, while a stream reserves repeating network capacity before sending begins. A stream's message size and timing must fit that reservation.

sections.title: Datagram Message Header
sections.content:
A datagram begins with six 16-bit header words, followed by up to 16,384 bits of user data. The header identifies the message, contains a checksum, and can carry acceptance or refusal information for traffic in the opposite direction.

Other fields identify the source and destination hosts and set message priority, requested reliability, a time-to-live value, and how to handle detected data errors. A message number of zero disables acceptance/refusal tracking for that message. A stream uses the same six-word header shape but places a Host Stream ID where a datagram carries priority and reliability settings.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message has a six-word header before its data. The header names the hosts and tells the network how to handle the message.

sections.title: Acceptance, Refusal and Flow Control
sections.content:
When acceptance/refusal (A/R) is enabled, the receiver reports whether it accepted a numbered datagram or stream message. A refusal includes a reason. A/R works independently in each direction, and up to 127 messages may be outstanding in each direction.

An acceptance means only that the receiver did not refuse the message; it does not guarantee that the network will deliver it. One A/R report can cover earlier numbered messages, and reports can be carried in a message going the other way. A/R can also be disabled for the whole link or for an individual message.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver can report that it accepted a message or refused it and give a reason. Acceptance does not promise that the network will deliver the message.

sections.title: Setting Up Streams and Groups
sections.content:
A host asks the network service host, at logical address zero, to create, change or delete streams and groups. A host request receives a reply and then the host acknowledges that reply. Request IDs distinguish exchanges that are still in progress.

A stream setup selects its allocation and transmission properties before the host sends stream data. Group setup assigns an address for sending to multiple hosts. The network can also notify a host when a stream or group changes and wait for an acknowledgment.
sections.plainLanguage: Before using a stream or group, a host sends a request to the network service host. The service host replies, and the host confirms that it received the reply.

sections.title: Link Startup, Checks and Loopback
sections.content:
HAP defines control messages for restarting a link, monitoring its operation, and testing it with loopback. Restart Request and Restart Complete messages coordinate initialization; the restart exchange also controls whether acceptance/refusal is enabled.

While the link is active, Status messages report counters and other operating information. A Loopback Request asks the other end to return the sender's messages, which helps test the host-to-SIMP connection. Other control messages can warn that a link is going down or carry no-operation data.

The preface calls HAP an experimental protocol expected to change as network capabilities and supported satellite systems evolve.
sections.plainLanguage: The host and switch exchange restart messages before normal operation. Later, status reports help them monitor the link, and a loopback request checks that messages can travel back.
